title: sufr reads its input through libsail's Reader and copies the residues itself
body:
`read_sequence_file` in `libsufr/src/build.rs` reads the input with needletail's `parse_fastx_file`. For each record it pushes the delimiter, records where the record starts, and copies `rec.seq()` into the text. It takes the record's name as the id up to its first whitespace. `normalize` then makes one more pass over the whole text. It maps every byte through a table for soft masking and records which bytes occur.

sufr-409cc8 asks whether `libsail` reads the input faster than needletail. This issue says how sufr would read through `libsail` if the answer is yes.

## Proposal

Use `libsail` the way nail uses it. `libsail` frames the records and names them. sufr turns each record's bytes into text itself.

- `libsail::index::Reader::new(file, Format::Fasta)` frames one record at a time out of a stream. `advance()` moves to the next record. `record()` returns that record's bytes, header line included. The reader keeps nothing per record.
- `libsail::seq::fasta::name_of(record)` returns the name. That is the header after `>` and any leading whitespace, up to the next whitespace. It returns `None` when the bytes do not open with `>`.
- sufr copies the residues itself. A residue is every byte after the first line that is not ASCII whitespace.

```rust
let mut reader = Reader::new(File::open(path)?, Format::Fasta);
while reader.advance()? {
    let record = reader.record();
    let name = name_of(record);
    let body = record
        .iter()
        .position(|&b| b == b'\n')
        .map_or(record.len(), |i| i + 1);
    text.extend(
        record[body..]
            .iter()
            .copied()
            .filter(|b| !b.is_ascii_whitespace()),
    );
}
```

nail reads its inputs this way. It never calls `libsail`'s `FastaParser::parse`. It parses a record's bytes with its own `Sequence::from_fasta`. The test `index_and_output_agree_on_record_names` in nail's `io/fasta.rs` checks nail's names against `name_of` on a set of awkward headers.

sufr keeps its fallback name for a record whose header has no name.

## Rejected

- `FastaParser::parse`. It returns a `FastaRecord` whose `seq` is a new `Vec` of the residues. sufr would copy every residue twice and allocate once per record.
- A `libsail` function that appends a record's residues to a buffer the caller owns. sail-56ab6e proposed it as `fasta::append_seq` and was dropped. sufr was its only caller. It could not apply sufr's byte table without a parameter that only sufr would use.

## Cost

- `libsail` reads neither FASTQ nor gzip, and needletail reads both today. `Reader::new` takes any `Read`, so sufr could hand it a gzip decoder. `libsail` has no FASTQ reader.
- sufr's copy and `FastaParser::parse` each decide which bytes are residues. Both drop ASCII whitespace today. A test in sufr that compares its text with the `seq` that `parse` returns on a few records would catch the two drifting apart.
- `Reader` holds the current record whole in its buffer. Peak memory grows by the largest record, which in hg38 is a chromosome.

## Open

- Whether the copy should apply the `normalize` table as it goes. That saves a pass over the text. `normalize` runs over the text in parallel chunks, though, and the copy runs on one thread. A timing on hg38noN would show which is faster.
- Whether sufr can drop FASTQ input, or keeps needletail for it.
